abstracts.008264: Research in formal theoretical semantics has recently expanded its scope to include gestural communication, focusing in particular on gestures that contribute to the content of an accompanying utterance, e.g., size gestures (LARGE, WIDE), pointing gestures, and gestures that depict objects (TELESCOPE) or actions (SLAP). At the same time, fruitful inquiries at the intersection of primatology and linguistics have given rise to the hypothesis that human and non-human great apes share a common set of directive (=imperative) gestures. Directive gestures such as STOP or COME-CLOSER, pose non-trivial issues for a semantic analysis: we inherit the challenges that pertain to the analysis of imperative utterances (Come closer!), while adding a further challenge that stems from the underspecified mapping between a directive body movement and its potential counterparts in human language. We begin by outlining the problem and surveying the nascent state-of-the-art with regards to a formal semantics of directive gestures. Particular attention is given to the multifunctionality of directive gestures, which typically have different effects in different contexts; for example, a non-human ape gesture may communicate "Stop that" in some contexts and "Move away" in others, with similar patterns found in humans. We show that this multifunctionality can be derived from a single, rich abstract lexical entry, "Not…!", a candidate for a universal building block of meaning, shared by human and non-human great apes. "Not…!", which incorporates negation/rejection, temporal reference and presuppositionality is more explanatory in comparison to a minimal alternative. This chapter lays out the hypothesis space, addressing the foundational question of how to explain attested gestural overlap between human and non-human great apes. We conclude the chapter by reviewing potential expansions of the analysis to the pragmatic gestures of humans, which are thus placed on the primate gestural meaning continuum and connected to the directive gestures we share with our non-human relatives in the great ape family.
abstracts.008655: This paper is about English exceptive-additive constructions introduced by ‘besides’. Like the better-studied pure exceptives introduced by ‘but’, ‘besides’ contributes an inference of exception when it occurs with quantifiers that exhibit universal force (e.g., ‘every’ or ‘no’). However, while exceptives are incompatible with quantifiers that have existential force, this is not the case for ‘besides’. In such contexts, ‘besides’ contributes an inference of addition. We propose a unified compositional account that explains the exceptive-additive behavior of ‘besides’ and its distinctions from exceptives like ‘but’. Our analysis extends the treatment of exceptives framed in terms of EXH (Gajewski 2013, Hirsch 2016, Crnič 2021) to exceptive-additives. We propose that, while both ‘besides’ and ‘but’ share a core contribution of domain subtraction, the methods for deriving alternatives differ between the two types of constructions. For quantificational claims with ‘but’, the alternatives are constructed by substituting the DP following ‘but’ with other DPs. In contrast, the only alternative for a quantificational claim with 'besides' that is distinct from the original claim has no subtraction at all. By reducing the set of alternatives, our account explains the compatibility of ‘besides’ with ‘exactly-n’ numerals and captures the additive inference observed in these cases. At the same time, it captures the exceptive-like behavior of ‘besides’ when paired with universal and negative quantifiers. To generalize this approach to all modified numerals, we adopt a decompositional theory of their semantics. According to this theory, modified numerals are treated as quantifiers over degrees that can optionally move at LF, leaving behind a constituent equivalent in meaning to an ‘exactly-n’ claim. We propose that the additive inference is computed under the scope of a numeral on this constituent. We suggest that a similar approach to the treatment of existential some can account for its interaction with ‘besides’. Finally, we extend our analysis to wh-questions, exploring the implications of applying EXH to weak answers.
abstracts.009273: Co-compounds (CC) are pairs of morphosyntactically parallel and semantically related elements that constitute a single morphosyntactic and semantic unit. Usually described as a type of (asyndetic) coordination in the typological literature, they have only received sporadic attention from generative syntacticians, and have mostly been analysed as a subtype of exocentric compounds (Scalise, Fábregas & Forza 2009). In contrast to this previous analysis, based on data from two Uralic languages (Hungarian and Surgut Khanty), we argue that co-compounding is a syntactic operation: an instance of two heads undergoing Merge and being dominated by a shared layer of functional projections. While an implicit assumption of endocentricity (Chomsky 1970) and the projection principle (Chomsky 1993) has been that it is exactly one head that heads and projects a phrase, we argue that as long as a few conditions (that CCs are subject to) are met, the existence of such two-headed phrases is unproblematic for the standard understanding of these two core concepts. We also address the issue of labelling that emerges when two heads undergo Merge in a symmetric fashion. We model the semantics of CCs in terms of substitution by a shared superordinate term plus universal or existential closure. We also address variation between Hungarian and Surgut Khanty in terms of (i) the required degree of semantic relatedness between the two elements and (ii) the availability of dual/plural marking and a conjunctive interpretation; we relate this variation to the very different functional load that co-compounding carries in the two languages.
abstracts.009514: Cognitive evolution is to cognitively represented systems what Darwinian evolution is to biological systems. Same problem structure, same solution structure.Therefore, the laws of the theory of evolution (Modern Synthesis and Population Genetics) are the laws of the descent of grammars and their development, as shown in this article.
abstracts.009559: The theory of semantic prosody posits that words acquire evaluative coloring through repeated collocation with positively or negatively charged contexts. While this usage-based framework effectively describes distributional patterns, it faces persistent theoretical challenges regarding directionality: does usage shape meaning, or does meaning shape usage? This paper demonstrates that for a significant class of frequently studied words, inherent lexical-semantic profiles act as primary filters that attract words to congruent discourse contexts, with collocational patterns emerging as consequences rather than causes of connotative meaning. Through systematic analysis of cause, utterly, commit, set in, foster, and regime, integrating published corpus analyses with theoretical linguistics, this study shows that their attested collocational skews reflect underlying semantic features—agentive, intensive, volitionally binding, gradual-onset, facilitative, and system-control profiles, respectively. Counterevidence from neutral and positive contexts in multiple corpora undermines claims of fixed evaluative prosodies while supporting profile-based explanations. Diachronic evidence demonstrates that semantic profiles remain stable across centuries even as specific collocational patterns vary, supporting the claim that profiles drive usage rather than absorbing evaluative charge from it. This reconceptualization addresses the problematic lexical-encyclopedic dichotomy, demonstrating through evidence from large language models, language testing, and cross-linguistic research that the traditional boundary between lexical meaning and world knowledge is far more permeable than conventional accounts acknowledge. The findings have practical implications for lexicography, natural language processing, and language pedagogy.
abstracts.009594: This paper challenges the traditional lexical-encyclopedic dichotomy in formal semantics by proposing that linguistic meaning and world-knowledge exist on a gradient of conventionalization rather than forming categorically distinct types of knowledge. Through an analysis of entailment strength and intersubjective agreement patterns, I argue that the field's persistent failure to theorize connotative meaning stems from systematically conflating two distinct phenomena: cultural connotation (systematic, community-level patterns that generate weak entailments) and private connotation (idiosyncratic, individual associations). Drawing on evidence from semantic prosody research, arbitrariness of the linguistic sign, language acquisition patterns, and computational modeling, I develop a gradient framework in which meaning components are distinguished by their level of conventionalization rather than by categorical membership in "denotative" versus "connotative". This reconceptualization provides theoretical tools for understanding how lexical semantic profiles generate systematic distributional patterns while remaining resistant to conscious introspection, thereby resolving longstanding puzzles in the relationship between word meaning and usage patterns.
abstracts.009649: Modal items are known to often show ambiguity with respect to modal flavor. For example, English 'can' can express both deontic and circumstantial flavor. To date, however, it remains unstudied whether there are particular sets of modal flavors that are more frequently colexified than others across the world’s languages. Here, we avail ourself of the recent database of Uegaki et al. (2024) to uncover natural classes of modal flavor colexification, and to evaluate the degree that these natural classes can be captured using different kinds of ontological structures.
abstracts.009660: This paper investigates two types of barest conditionals in Mandarin, both characterized by their minimal clausal structure and the presence of identical pairing, i.e., two duplicated verbs, such as Gāi chī chī, gāi hē hē ‘Eat when it's time to eat, drink when it's time to drink’, or wh-phrases, like Ài shéi shéi ‘Whoever it may be’ (cf. Tsai 2025). Based on the identical pairing analysis, this paper argues that both types are licensed by an explicit necessity operator, namely the sentence-initial modal: It unselectively binds the pair of identical variables, thereby licensing the donkey-conditional in question (cf. Cheng & Huang 1996, 2020). On the other hand, the type of identical pairing (i.e., verb vs. wh-phrase) depends on which variable acts as the information focus, while the sentence-initial modal serves to license the barest conditional construal. Furthermore, we argue that prosodic fusion, which merges the two separate conditional clauses into a single sentential intonation phrase (cf. Feng 2017), is key to identifying barest conditionals: Only after the fusion do the sentences need to observe the strict requirement of identical pairing. Finally, this paper brings to light the fascinating interaction among register, syntax, and prosody as observed in the formation of barest conditionals.
abstracts.009667: Creating high-quality phonological representations in academic documents is often time-consuming and requires juggling multiple tools and LaTeX packages (most notably TikZ). This vignette introduces phonokit, an open-source Typst package designed to streamline the creation of phonological structures while maintaining typographical precision. The package provides intuitive functions for IPA transcription (supporting tipa input conventions), IPA vowel charts and consonant tables with built-in language inventories and flexible arrows, prosodic representations (syllables, feet, prosodic words, metrical grids), sonority profiles, autosegmental phonology (feature spreading, tone, delinking), multi-tier representations for complex non-linear structures such as Government Phonology and CV phonology, feature geometry, SPE feature matrices, Optimality Theory tableaux, Harmonic Grammar, Noisy Harmonic Grammar, Maximum Entropy grammars, and Hasse diagrams for constraint rankings. All functions prioritize minimal input syntax while automatically handling complex typographical challenges such as dynamic spacing, line crossing prevention, and proper alignment. phonokit aims to reduce cognitive load in document preparation, allowing phonologists to focus on content rather than formatting. The package is freely available through Typst's package repository and is under active development.
abstracts.009689: This paper proposes a unified framework that reconceives the relationship between lexical meaning and world knowledge as a gradient of conventionalization rather than a categorical distinction. Meaning components are distinguished by their level of conventionalization, operationalized as degree of speaker agreement, rather than by membership in "lexical" versus "encyclopedic" categories. The framework introduces a five-level gradient — reference, denotation, sense, cultural connotation, private connotation — corresponding to decreasing intersubjective agreement, and a typology of entailments (strong, default, weak) correlated with these levels. This reconceptualization clarifies semantic prosody, explains why some arguments converge while others polarize, and connects lexical semantics to social epistemology. Central to the epistemological application is the diagnosis of alpha misattribution: the error of treating a term whose meaning is genuinely low-agreement as though it carried the stability of a high-agreement term, an error that converts unresolved conceptual disagreement into the appearance of bad-faith resistance to consensus. The framework generates testable predictions about semantic change, argument dynamics, and the conditions under which making agreement levels explicit can reduce polarization.
abstracts.009693: Interest in animal communication has arguably reached an all-time high, with two very visible projects—the search for the animal roots of human language and the development of methods and technologies to decode animal signals. These projects need a shared, overarching scientific framework. We propose that animal linguistics offers one, which will require close collaboration between ethologists, linguists and, increasingly, AI specialists. One possible way to view the project—not the only one—goes as follows. With the same ambition as human formal linguistics, animal linguistics seeks to develop explicit models of animal communication ("formal animal linguistics"), to understand the extent and limits of variation in living species ("comparative animal linguistics"), and to investigate the cognitive basis of observed properties ("animal psycholinguistics"). Through a "phylogenetic tree of animal signals", it seeks to retrace and explain the path from ancestral signals to modern ones ("evolutionary animal linguistics"). In its synchronic and diachronic components, animal linguistics offers an integrative framework for scientific and technological progress in animal communication. Going forward, it could offer new areas of application and new sources of insight for multiple areas of cognitive science.
abstracts.009712: Embedding material under intensional operators gives rise to a variety of `non-de dicto' construals: the proposition seemingly expressed by the embedded clause does not describe subject’s the attitudinal state, yet the sentence can be judged true. This paper makes three contributions: First, we strengthen the claims by Mayr & Schmitt 2024 that non-de dicto construals are a uniform phenomenon, which does not involve dedicated syntactic structures or morphology: The distinction between de dicto and non-de dicto construals does not involve ambiguity but, and this is our second point, arises from properties of meaning per se. What can be described as `replacement' -- in non-de dicto construals the meaning of a constituent of the embedded clause is replaced by another -- results from meanings being underspecified: any expression introduces a set of meanings and intensional operators existentially quantify over such sets.s the underspecification we assume is more radical as in underspecification accounts of other phenomena, we propose a new mechanism constraining it, roughly based on pragmatic considerations. Discourse participants aim for `discourse stability': the `traditional' meanings of expressions and their replacements must be indistinguishable for all the questions that might occur in the projected discourse.
abstracts.009841: This paper presents the first systematic description of headless relative clauses in Tigrinya (Semitic; Eritrea and Ethiopia; SOV). Drawing on novel fieldwork data, it examines three types of headless relatives, namely light-headed, super-free, and free-choice relatives. The data show that, unlike many other languages, Tigrinya forms both headed and headless relative clauses using the same morphosyntactic strategy, which involves the relativizer z(ɨ)- without overt wh-elements. Headless relatives in Tigrinya do not rely on interrogative wh-structures, in contrast to languages such as English. Notably, free relatives are not attested. Instead, all headless relative clauses share a structural core with headed relatives, differing only in the presence or absence of nominal and determiner layers. By documenting this pattern, the paper identifies a previously underdescribed strategy in Afro-Asiatic. These findings refine the typology of relativization, provide empirical evidence for cross-linguistic variation in relative clause formation, and establish a foundation for formal analyses of Tigrinya and related languages.
abstracts.009914: In the Box Theory proposed by Chomsky (2024) and extended by Kitahara and Seely (2025), successive-cyclic movement is eliminated and wh-displacement is analyzed as phase-level access from CQ for Externalization. Based on this framework, this article argues that island conditions in English such as the Subject Condition, the Adjunct Condition, the Wh-Island Condition, and the Complex NP Condition is unified into a locality constraint on Externalization to the effect that CQ cannot not externalize a wh-phrase within a previous phase cycle associated with ‘clausal’ interpretation (i.e., a phase in a theta-bar position or a CP phase headed by an interrogative/relative complementizer). This article also argues that the proposed analysis accounts for island repair and lack thereof in sluicing and VP-ellipsis.
abstracts.009987: Honorifics across languages tend to recruit specific phi-features (e.g. plural and 3rd person) for polite reference to the addressee. Wang (2023) derives this regularity pragmatically from the interaction between Maximize Presupposition! and a Taboo of Directness over the presuppositionally weak features "plural" and "3rd person". We argue that this account both undergenerates and overgenerates. It cannot accommodate the typological asymmetries between 1st and 2nd person (e.g. the absence of speaker-inclusive 2PL), the role-specific use-conditions attached to forms like English Nurse We, the disappearance of honorific content under ellipsis, or the lexeme-specific contrasts seen, e.g., in Spanish nosotros vs. null pro. We propose a hybrid pragmatic-conventional alternative. Person and number are treated not as presuppositional heads but as components of complex anaphoric indices, with their semantic import encoded as constraints on admissible assignment functions. Assuming this system, we derive a markedness hierarchy 2 < 1 < 3 over indices defined by referential explicitness. A valence-neutral Taboo of Distance favors weak indices for the expression of social or psychological distance, while language-specific use-conditional constraints license particular weak indices in particular utterance contexts. Crucially, a conjunctive definition of semantic information over both truth-conditional and use-conditional dimensions allows weak indices enriched by conventional use-conditions to survive Quantity-based competition with their more explicit alternatives, dissolving the apparent conflict between informativity and indirectness. The result accommodates 1st person addresse honorifics, anti-honorific uses of the same features, and the existence of lexical idiosyncrasies in honorific inventories.
abstracts.009998: This paper applies the gradient conventionalization framework developed in Mozahid (2025a, 2025b, 2026) to the architecture of artificial intelligence systems, arguing that the persistent divide between statistical and categorical AI is fundamentally a semantic phenomenon rather than an engineering one. The framework operationalizes meaning components through levels of intersubjective agreement (α), providing a principled account of why different AI architectures can process only certain ranges of the α-gradient. Categorical systems operate exclusively at α→1.0; large language models (LLMs) operate across α=0.30–0.95, most reliably in the α=0.70–0.90 zone of default entailment. α-level assignments are derived from corpus-distributional measures established independently in Mozahid (2025a), treating AI behavioral data as a convergent test rather than the source of those assignments — a methodological structure that resolves a potential circularity and transforms divergences between predicted and observed AI behavior into theoretically informative evidence. The architectural mapping yields four contributions: it reframes LLM hallucination as α-level misassignment, the structural mismatch between assertoric output form and probabilistic generative mechanism; it reframes neuro-symbolic hybrid systems as implicitly α-stratified architectures whose routing criterion should be α-level rather than domain or task type; it argues that formal systems are natural language driven to α→1.0 through definitional stipulation, connecting the framework to debates in the philosophy of mathematics; and it identifies α-elevation — conventionalization's upward pressure on intersubjective agreement — as a theoretical concept currently absent from AI architecture research but necessary for any principled account of how formal reasoning emerges from natural language processing.
abstracts.010012: This paper proposes that encyclopedic knowledge — what we know about the world, as distinct from what follows from definitions or logical structure — consists fundamentally of conventionalized arbitrary relations. Drawing on Saussurean sign-arbitrariness, Kripkean modal semantics, and the gradient conventionalization framework developed in prior work on lexical meaning, the paper argues that every empirical claim depends on a contingent carving of reality into concepts and a contingent act of reference-fixing that anchors those concepts to worldly entities. Both operations are arbitrary in the Saussurean sense and require intersubjective stabilization before they can function as publicly warranted knowledge rather than as private epistemic state. The thesis is tested against apparent counterexamples — Kripke's necessary a posteriori, scientific laws, mathematical truths, and perceptual beliefs — each reducing to either a system-internal relation or a conventionalized arbitrary relation not necessary in any world-independent sense. The degree to which a claim qualifies as publicly warranted knowledge corresponds to its degree of conventionalization within a specified epistemic community, operationalized through the alpha coefficient developed in prior work. The framework remains agnostic about inaccessible first-person standpoints, a stance illustrated through wrongly convicted defendants, deceased persons, and the Cartesian cogito. Philosophy, on the resulting picture, is not a producer of α-scorable knowledge but the generative substrate through which the conceptual carvings over which conventionalization operates are invented, contested, and revised.
abstracts.010037: This paper re-examines self-destructive feeding, a type of overapplication opacity, and proposes a new analysis based on the commonalities shared by all attested cases. It is found that all the four cases of self-destructive feeding found in Turkish, Javanese and Japanese involve rules with non-derived environment blocking and attempt to resolve consonant clusters by making changes to the suffix. Based on these common characteristics, a unified analysis is provided to account for not only the self-destructive feeding pattern but also its related phenomena simultaneously, with the help of underspecification and positional/contextual faithfulness under Parallel Optimality Theory. Finally, it is argued that self-destructive feeding is an epiphenomenon of phonologically-conditioned allomorphy.
abstracts.010058: On the surface, English [Q+where] forms such as everywhere are locative. Yet as Sluckin & Kastner (forthcoming) document experimentally, they can also serve as impersonal human subjects, as in Everywhere in the UK loves Marmite, in which everywhere = everyone. The form retains its locative morphology and the pro-form where, yet it binds they/their and controls like a [+HUMAN] quantified indefinite pronoun. It must also be distinguished from ordinary locative (every place) and metonymic institutional readings. We argue that the impersonal use emerges from a distinct syntactic configuration in the nominal domain, rather than from lexical polysemy. Where spells out a higher locative D/P shell, while beneath it sits a silent, sortal, human-descriptive root √PERSON, selected by a relational categorising head nCAT bearing [uPlace]. Relationality comes from the categoriser, not from the root (cf. Adger 2013). The [uPlace] feature forces an overt locative PP into Spec,nPCAT, where it saturates the place argument of an inhabitant relation; nEA then abstracts over the human variable, and the quantifier binds the resulting property. Because the root receives its zero exponent locally under this categoriser, rather than from the higher shell, its human content remains active though unpronounced. Institutional everywhere, by contrast, retains a √PLACE structure with contextual transfer. The obligatory locative PP follows from [uPlace], whereas the macro-geographic restriction is an interface condition rather than a syntactic feature.
abstracts.010060: Manuscripts under peer review are confidential materials, and as such, major publishers prohibit reviewers from uploading them to commercial generative AI systems. The current experiments tested whether the current AI systems consistently comply with this policy, and showed that this is not necessarily the case. In Experiment 1, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini rarely explained confidentiality when a first-time reviewer requested general help (2/30 trials). When the user explicitly asked whether a manuscript could be shared, ChatGPT accepted in 10/10 trials and Claude in 6/10, whereas Gemini consistently refused with a confidentiality warning. However, in Experiment 2, given a very similar prompt but with an attached manuscript, Gemini analyzed the attached file without warning in all 10 trials, suggesting the instability of its safeguard system. Further, Experiment 3a found that Gemini sometimes accepted sharing when prompted in Japanese. The result of this exploratory experiment motivated a confirmatory experiment (Experiment 3b), which directly compared English and Japanese. As predicted, Gemini accepted sharing more often in Japanese (27/30) than in English (1/30). Taken together, the current findings show that an apparently reliable confidentiality safeguard may fail when the request format or language changes, underscoring the need to test whether the AI's “ethical” responses generalize across conditions.
abstracts.010142: Fonology is an R package for phonological analysis, with tools for grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, syllabification, stress assignment, sonority-based measures, natural-class feature matrices, and maximum entropy modeling. It provides primary support for Portuguese, Spanish, French, and Italian, and English transcription that allows user-correctable overrides and heuristic fallback for out-of-vocabulary forms. Accuracy of grapheme-phoneme conversion ranges from 94% to 99% (using a combination of lookup and regex). Functions are vectorized, which yields fast performance over large texts (fast for R, that is). The package is designed to support reproducible phonological research and teaching by integrating common analytical workflows into a consistent R interface, including transcription, feature-based generalization, quantitative phonotactic measures, and visualization-ready outputs.
abstracts.010161: The theory of semantic prosody holds that words acquire evaluative coloring through repeated collocation with charged contexts, such that connotation is absorbed from usage rather than encoded in the lexicon. This paper argues that the phenomena motivating that theory are real but have been correctly measured and incorrectly attributed. It treats lexical meaning as a weighted bundle of semantic features and distinguishes two independent readouts of that bundle: a structural axis, tracking coverage of a word's non-evaluative content, and a valence axis, tracking its evaluative content specifically. The prosody tradition has read collocational skew almost exclusively onto the valence axis; this paper argues that for a substantial class of frequently studied words the skew belongs on the structural axis instead, and that this misattribution, not any failure to detect real pattern, is the source of the tradition's most persistent unsolved problems. Through analysis of cause, utterly, commit, set in, foster, and regime, alongside the contrasting case of murder, the paper develops a falsification procedure — the contradiction test — for locating a feature's conventionalization: features admitting structured, unmarked counterexamples are diagnosed as weak; those admitting none, as strong. The six classical words encode strongly conventionalized structural profiles alongside weak valence content, while murder's valence sits strong, fused with its descriptive content. The account answers two problems named in the prosody literature — the introspection problem and the causal-direction problem — and distinguishes its diagnostic claim from gradient absorption accounts, which tolerate exceptions but lack a mechanism for locating them.
abstracts.010243: Interpreting quality can shape how an asylum applicant's account is understood, while UK inspection and guidance documents continue to identify challenges involving language matching, interpreter preparation and quality assurance. This pilot study operationalises translation literacy as explicit reflection on translation choices, semantic range, alternatives, evidence, consequences and evaluation. Twenty-one Arabic-English bilingual adults completed unguided pre- and post-framework translation-evaluation tasks after guided exposure either to TRACE, a five-step mnemonic reflection scaffold, or to an active structured control checklist. Eighty-four responses were scored on a six-dimension rubric by the original marker and three independent blinded raters; analyses used the mean of the four ratings. TRACE did not produce a statistically significant advantage over control on combined change scores (TRACE +1.48/24; control +2.33/24; U=47.0, p=.597). Alternatives showed the clearest TRACE-aligned descriptive pattern, but the between-group change difference was non-significant. The findings therefore do not establish TRACE superiority or a general causal effect of structured reflection. They instead identify a feasible measurement approach and hypotheses for larger, better-balanced studies using professional interpreters, delayed retention testing and spoken high-stakes tasks.
abstracts.010299: This study proposes a unified morphosyntactic–semantic account of the suffixal form -re found in the EMJ realis paradigm — the so-called izenkei — and related phenomena. It argues that -re is a contextual allomorph of the inflexional suffix -ru, which marks a clause as [0PAST, +ACTUAL-WORLD-COMMITMENT] and thereby presents the eventuality expressed by that clause as belonging to the actual world lato sensu. It surfaces as -re when the clause is set as a premise. This premise-setting environment is supplied overtly by the suffixes -ba [+CONDITIONAL] and -do(mo) [+CONCESSIVE], and covertly by the phonologically null suffix -Ø [+PREM(ISE-SETTING)] in the =koso type of kakari-musubi. Thus, the focus particle =koso does not itself condition the allomorphy -ru → -re, but merely focalises a constituent not containing the finite predicate within a clause already set as a premise by -Ø [+PREM]. In the =zo/=namu type, by contrast, a clause with a topic–comment articulation is first constructed, and its topic constituent containing the finite predicate is nominalised by -Ø [+NOM(INAL)] so that it can be treated as a topic NP. The focus particle =zo or =namu is then added to the comment. The resulting construction is analysed as a COPULA-LESS INVERTED PSEUDO-CLEFT in which the comment/focus precedes the nominalised topic/background without the intervention of the pseudo-copula =n-ari. This pseudo-cleft has two further types: the =ka type and the =ya type. The distribution of the focus particles is simple: in an interrogative clause, =ka is selected if an interrogative phrase constitutes the focus, whereas =ya is selected if a non-interrogative phrase constitutes the focus; in a declarative clause, =zo/=namu is selected. Cross-linguistically, Spanish and Portuguese provide close structural parallels to the =zo/=namu, =ya and =ka types. The =koso type, by contrast, contains no such nominalised topic phrase containing a finite predicate and is therefore NOT a PSEUDO-CLEFT. NOR does there seem to be any syntactic evidence that it is an IT-CLEFT. Finally, the absence of a special predicate form with the focus particles =ha and =mo follows from the set-based nature of their focalisation, which presupposes a contextually relevant set rather than a clause set as a premise by -Ø [+PREM]. Furthermore, in these constructions, no constituent containing a finite predicate constitutes the topic, and hence no such constituent is nominalised by -Ø [+NOM] to form a topic NP. Accordingly, the particles themselves do not determine the predicate forms. Rather, the configuration is constructed FIRST and only THEN determines both the predicate form and which focus particle may occur. Traditional particle–predicate concord called kakari-musubi is therefore reanalysed as a surface correspondence between two consequences of the same independently constructed structure.
abstracts.010337: This paper examines several understudied and unusual types of copular constructions in Polish, in which the copula agrees with the predicate rather than the subject. It argues that this seemingly unexpected agreement pattern follows from a well-known principle: the controller of agreement is the highest accessible phrase in the domain of agreement. This conclusion is defended against appearances, which suggest that the controller of agreement is not the highest accessible phrase in the constructions at hand. In the process, the paper advances several theoretical claims, including the proposal that the demonstrative found in the subject position in such constructions is structurally reduced and lacks a case projection, that certain non-agreeing leftmost phrases are base-generated above TP, and that there are two flavours of Pred in Polish, including a highly defective Pred which combines with nominal predicates in the nominative instead of the usual instrumental of predication. The paper also reports the discovery of long-distance agreement in Polish, apparently not noted so far in the context of Slavic.

abstracts.010391: My previous studies have demonstrated that current AI systems can readily assist users in performing questionable research practices (QRPs) when prompted to do so. This paper shifts the focus from documenting the problem to developing a solution. Five experiments tested whether custom instructions---short texts that users can paste into their AI settings---can serve as a "vaccine" against AI-assisted QRPs in Gemini. Experiment 1 found that both a conceptual-level instruction (referring to QRPs in general) and a behavior-list instruction (enumerating specific prohibited practices) reduced Gemini's willingness to p-hack from 100% to 0% across 30 trials each. With 30 pre-registered follow-up trials, the behavior-list instruction maintained a 0% execution rate across 60 trials in total, placing the one-sided 95% upper confidence bound on its execution rate below 5%. Experiments 2a&b showed that the same instruction generalized to optional stopping, post-hoc outlier exclusion and data fabrication by blocking these requests in all 20 out of 20 trials for each task, though it failed to block a missing value imputation request in one out of 20 trials. Experiments 3a&b demonstrated that the custom instruction written in English remained effective when the user's prompt was in Japanese. Taken together, the results show that a very simple, user-level intervention can (almost) categorically eliminate a wide range of AI-assisted QRPs under the tested conditions. The vaccine is provided in a copy-and-pastable format for immediate use.
abstracts.010472: This paper proposes a novel syntactic analysis of English resultative constructions within the framework of modern Minimalist syntax (Chomsky 2024; Kitahara and Seely 2025). Challenging traditional Small Clause analyses, we argue that the result predicate is accommodated within a functional phrase, PredP (Bowers 1993), separating the state-holder from the main verb's direct object position. Combined with the FormCopy operation and Minimal Search, our model accounts for the long-standing WH-extraction asymmetry between paint-type and consider-type resultatives. Specifically, we demonstrate that consider-type verbs lack a lexical object position (DP2), preventing FormCopy from generating the required search path for WH-extraction. This structural difference naturally derives the extraction restriction without positing ad-hoc constraints, offering a unified account of syntactic relations and semantic interpretations in resultative constructions.
abstracts.010475: The placement of prosodic prominence in an answer is generally taken to depend on the question. E.g., "Who saw Mary? BEN saw Mary", but "Who did Ben see? Ben saw MARY". This correspondence is referred to as congruence, and in much of the literature it is captured in terms of grammatical machinery and constraints. I argue that such grammatical explanations are unnecessary in light of pragmatic considerations governing discourse, primarily those concerning the role of pragmatic questions, understood in terms of partitions. These considerations derive a more accurate empirical picture of question-answer felicity and do so in terms of general assumptions rather than specialized machinery.
abstracts.010476: Previous reconstructions of Middle Chinese posit Ming (明母) as [m], Wei (微母) as the labiodental nasal [ɱ], and Fu (敷母) as [pfʰ]. The latter two values, however, are hardly attested in modern Chinese dialects—a situation at odds with the general pattern that Chinese dialects preserve Middle Chinese features widely. Drawing on Dunhuang Sino-Tibetan transcriptions, the 'Phags-pa transcriptions in the Menggu Ziyun, historical foreign transcriptions, and modern dialectal databases, this paper proposes a new reconstruction: Ming as the prenasalized voiced bilabial stop [ᵐb]; Wei as the bilabial nasal [m], arising through the unconditioned change ᵐb > m and established as an independent initial through Song-dynasty standardization within the closed third-division slot; Fu as the voiceless glottal fricative [h]; and Feng (奉母) as the labiodental voiced fricative [v]. Re-examining the initial table prefaced to the Menggu Ziyun, the paper argues that Zhu Zongwen's double assignment of the letter ꡤ to Fei (非母) and Feng reflects the loss of the Qieyun Ming value in the Yuan phonological system and the resulting merger of Wei and Ming; the corrected assignments are ꡏ = Wei [m], ꡓ = Feng [v], ꡤ = Fu [hu], and ꡰ = Fei [f]. Dialectal evidence includes the acoustic agreement between [ᵐb] in Ming-initial words of Taiwan Southern Min and the Dunhuang transcription letter འབ (ɦb), the geographical distribution of [h] readings of labial words in Southeastern dialects corroborating the Menggu Ziyun transcriptions, and the zero-initial breathy-voiced rhymes of the Zhongyuan Yinyun ("房防", "墳焚棼", "扶夫蚨符芙鳬浮"), which furnish synchronic minimal pairs. On this basis we propose the Breathy-Voice Accommodation Hypothesis: the phonetic origin of the light labials is a zero-initial breathy-voiced closed rhyme formed when labial initials were lost from Bang and Pang words of the closed third division—words that in the dominant phonological system already belonged to the Bing class of clear-consonant-with-murmur syllables after medial loss. Subsequent developments depend on each dialect's capacity to accommodate breathy voice: accommodating systems retain the zero-initial breathy rhyme; non-accommodating systems substitute [v] or [hu], with [v] later devoicing to [f]. Wei [m] alone is the natural outcome of Ming [ᵐb], independent of this contact-driven evolution.
abstracts.010477: This paper discusses the etymology of the Old Chinese word for “horse” (*mˤraʔ). Based on the distribution of Indo-European *markos, the phonological rules of Yeniseian (Starostin, personal communication, 2026), and the Sintashta-Karasuk archaeological evidence, this paper proposes that *markos entered Old Chinese through a Yeniseian intermediary. Phonologically, this is reflected in the direct correspondence of m-, the deletion of -o (Yeniseian final-vowel deletion), the weakening of -k to a glottal stop, and the loss of -s. The archaeological chain is Volga-Don → Sintashta → Andronovo → Karasuk → Shang. The paper also responds to Bjørn’s(2022) Iranian bāraka- hypothesis, pointing out its phonological ad hocness (b- → m-) and chronological problems. It argues that loanword studies must be constrained by archaeology. This is a working paper; comments are welcome. 本文探讨上古汉语“马”（mˤraʔ）的词源问题。基于印欧语*markos 的分布、叶尼 塞语系的音系规则、以及辛塔什塔-卡拉苏克考古证据，本文提出：*markos 经叶尼塞语系中 介传入上古汉语，音系上表现为 m-直接对应、-o 脱落（叶尼塞删尾规则）、-k 弱化为喉塞、 -s 脱落。考古学链条为伏尔加河-顿河—辛塔什塔—安德罗诺沃—卡拉苏克—殷商。本文同 时回应 Bjørn（2022）的伊朗语 bāraka-假说，指出其音系特设（*b-→m-）和可能存在的时 间错位问题。本文认为，借词研究必须受考古学约束。本文为工作论文，欢迎批评指正。
abstracts.010478: This paper re-examines the status of the so-called “secondary emphatics” in Arabic dialects: consonants traditionally considered to be marginal phonemes with limited emphasis spread effects. These include labial /b, m, f/, coronal /r, l, n/ and velar /k, x/ consonants, among others. An analysis of their phonological behaviour across varieties reveals that only /r/ and /l/ enjoy a phonemic status in certain dialects. The remaining consonants are characterized by a very low functional load, near-exclusive occurrence in loanwords, and strict adjacency to a low vowel, thus casting doubt on their classification as phonemes. An alternative proposal is to treat this behaviour as evidence of a phonemic split in the low vowels, distinguishing front /a/ from a new emphatic vowel /ɑ/. This approach eliminates the need to posit marginal phonemes and generates an economical system, where the new ɑ/ɑ shares a secondary place [dorsal] feature with emphatic consonants.
abstracts.010479: The Tigris qeltu-dialects are known to have a uvular fricative ġ in place of historical rāʔ, but existing side by side with a tapped r, and their occurrence is both phonologically and sociolinguistically conditioned. This chapter first outlines the sociolinguistic variation, but then concentrates on the phonological behavior of (inclusive) R in three dialects of this qeltu subgroup, namely, Maṣlāwi Arabic and Christian and Jewish Baghdadi Arabic, based on data collected from four native informants via two reading tasks. The objective is to examine the lexical categories, distributional patterns, and possible phonological processes in which R participates, such as loan vs. native words, minimal pairs, cooccurrence restrictions on consonant combinations, and various types of assimilation. Although the data exhibit discrepancies between the dialects, evidence confirms the existence of two R phonemes in all three of them: a dorsal fricative /ġ/ which is a reflex of old rāʔ merged with inherited ġayn, and a coronal sonorant /r/ found mainly in loanwords and some native words with specifiable phonological contexts. A representational analysis, formulated in the framework of feature geometry, demonstrates that /r/ is exclusively rhotic while /ġ/ is not.
abstracts.010480: This paper examines the phonological systems of Bambara and English from a contrastive linguistic perspective, with particular attention to their implications for language teaching and learning. Bambara, a major Mande language spoken primarily in Mali, and English differ considerably in their sound inventories, vowel systems, syllable structures, tonal and stress patterns, and phonological processes. These differences may create pronunciation difficulties for Bambara-speaking learners of English, particularly in the production of English vowel contrasts, consonant clusters, word stress, and intonation. Similarly, English-speaking learners of Bambara may experience difficulties in recognizing and producing lexical tones, vowel nasalization, and other distinctive phonological features of the language. Drawing on Contrastive Analysis Theory and relevant descriptions of both languages, this paper identifies major phonological similarities and differences and discusses their pedagogical implications. It argues that systematic phonological comparison can help teachers anticipate learners' difficulties, develop appropriate instructional materials, and adopt teaching strategies that address specific pronunciation challenges. The paper concludes that explicit phonological instruction, listening discrimination, articulatory practice, and the integration of oral language activities are essential for improving pronunciation and communicative competence in both languages.

abstracts.010482: This paper presents an independent working hypothesis proposing that the structural similarities observed across the Altaic language family—including Turkic, Mongolic, Tungusinic, Koreanic, Japonic, and Ainu languages—serve as structural traces of an original ancestral language. By examining the inherent stability of language structures over borrowed vocabulary, this paper argues that uninterrupted geographical transmission chains (such as those across the Eurasian steppe) favor the preservation of deep structural features. Consequently, despite external lexical shifts, core grammatical architectures remain remarkably resilient, offering a new perspective on macro-family relationships and linguistic evolution.
abstracts.010483: In Mandarin Chinese, adjectives can modify nouns in two ways: (i) an adjective combines directly with a noun (A-N structure), or (ii) an adjective combines with the marker DE, and the resulting constituent modifies the nominal spine (A-DE-N structure). These two constructions exhibit a distributional asymmetry regarding simple and complex adjectives: while simple adjectives can appear in both structures, complex adjectives require the marker DE to modify a noun. This paper pursues two main goals. First, we investigate the morphosyntactic status of the two structures on the basis of their syntactic and semantic properties. We argue that A-DE-N structures are phrasal, whereas A-N structures result from morphological concatenation. Second, we develop an analysis that accounts for the attested distributional patterns and formalises the interpretational differences between A-N and A-DE-N structures. Our analysis further addresses the behaviour of reduplicated adjectives in Mandarin Chinese.
abstracts.010484: Abstract: This paper is an extension of the working paper “The Origin of the Old Chinese Word for‘horse’: An Indo-European Loanword Hypothesis via a Yeniseian Intermediary.” The Tibeto-Burman words for “horse” are formally divergent—Tibetan rta, rGyalrong mbrō, and Limbu ən—and are difficult to correlate with one another; they also cannot be phonologically matched with Chinese **mˤraʔ*. Combining Zhang et al.’s (2019) data on the divergence depth of Tibeto-Burman, Lyonnet’s (2021) archaeological study of the BMAC, and the material evidence for the southward migration of the Sintashta-Andronovo culture, this paper proposes that the Tibeto-Burman word for “horse” may have been transmitted through a BMAC intermediary. As the area of most intensive contact between southern Central Asia and steppe populations ca. 2200–1500 BCE, the BMAC is the most likely intermediary on chronological, geographical, and archaeological grounds. Since the linguistic affiliation of the BMAC remains uncertain, this paper does not attempt to reconstruct a proto-form; rather, it argues primarily from archaeological evidence for the plausibility of the BMAC as an intermediary. This is a working paper; comments are welcome. 摘要：本文是工作论文“上古汉语“马”的来源——一个经叶尼塞语系中介的印欧语借词假说”的延伸讨论。藏缅语族“马”词形式迥异：藏语 rta、嘉绒语 mbrō、林布语ən，彼此难以对应，亦与汉语 mˤraʔ在音系上无法匹配。本文结合张梦翰等（2019）关于藏缅语分化深度的数据、Lyonnet（2021）对 BMAC 的考古学研究，以及辛塔什塔-安德罗诺沃文化南迁的物质证据提出：藏缅语的“马”词可能经 BMAC 中介传入。BMAC 作为约公元前 2200–1500 年间中亚南部与草原人群接触最密集的区域，在时间、地理和考古证据上都是最可能的中介。由于BMAC 语言归属尚不明确，本文不试图重构原始形式，而主要从考古学角度论证 BMAC 作为中介的合理性。本文为工作论文，欢迎批评。
abstracts.010485: When people learn a new language, they learn more than its grammar. They may also learn what its speakers usually leave unsaid. I tested this idea with the LnNor Corpus, in which the same Polish speakers told picture stories in Polish, in English (their second language) and in Norwegian (their third). Twenty-nine had learned English and Norwegian in the classroom; twenty-three had learned them by living in Norway. Classroom learners often stated what the characters wanted (the cat wants the fish), and did so more in English and Norwegian than in Polish. Learners who lived in Norway also stated it freely in Polish, but almost never in English or Norwegian (p < .001 and p = .002). There they described only the attempt (the cat tries to catch the fish) and left the goal to be inferred, as native speakers did. Three further tests clarify the pattern. It was not carried over from the speakers' first or second language: it followed where the languages had been learned. It was not explained by speakers treating the task as a picture description. And it went with fluency, not with signs of difficulty. Read through Relevance Theory and Learnable Theory, leaving the goal implicit is an efficient choice, learned from the community that speaks the language. The results are exploratory, and I propose a replication and physiological tests of whether listeners reconstruct the unstated goal.
abstracts.010486: This paper investigates whether the generation of contrastive inferences depends on the at-issue status of a modifier or on its semiotic status. We report a German adaptation of the picture-selection paradigm developed by Alsop et al. (2018) and extend it to include pro-speech gestures. Participants completed a picture-selection task with three experimental conditions (lexical modifiers, pro-speech gestures, and co-speech gestures). In addition, each list contained unmodified baseline items that were not part of the factorial design. The results revealed a gradient pattern: lexical modifiers elicited the highest rate of contrastive interpretations, followed by pro-speech gestures and co-speech gestures. At the same time, both gesture conditions yielded substantially more contrastive interpretations than the control condition. We argue that these findings support a gradient, context-sensitive view of at-issueness while at the same time challenging accounts that exclude depictive meaning from alternative-based reasoning.
abstracts.010487: This dissertation investigates the floating quantifiers phenomenon, aiming to solve cases in which a universal quantifier surfaces separated from its associate nominal while preserving a tight interpretive equivalence, focusing on Arabic kull and English all. Building on the DP-hypothesis and a layered nominal architecture, the dissertation advances the central claim that universal quantifiers are best analyzed as D-heads inside DP, rather than as VP-adjunct adverbs or as Q-heads of a QP layer. Under this view, the quantifier and its associate are not autonomous phrases, they form a unified constituent, and the surface ‘adverbial-like’ placements characteristic of floating are derived via nominal movement that strands the quantifier in an intermediate landing position. Empirically, Arabic morphosyntax is leveraged as a decisive diagnostic through its agreement morphology and pronominal clitics in floated configurations, constituency and dependency predictions are tested. Arabic provides evidence for constituency, landing positions, and a canonical post-verbal clause-final Q position, base-generating the quantifier and it associate in the verbal domain. To address cross-linguistic variation, such as the availability of clause-final floated quantifiers in Arabic but not in English, the dissertation proposes a derivational model that (i) identifies a universal canonical base-position for Q and its associate DP in the verbal spine, (ii) restricts the derivation to a constrained set of landing sites and movement paths, and (iii) captures language differences via ON/OFF switch settings that license or block specific surface realizations of Q and its DP. Finally, this dissertation moves toward a broader account of the DP Hypothesis by arguing that DP structure should be maintained even in determiner-less languages. Together with the proposed account of quantifier’s canonical base-position, movement and stranding, this DP-based view aims to contribute to a unified analysis of floating quantifiers across languages. While the dissertation does not claim to establish a universal theory of floating quantifiers, it aims toward a more general, potentially universal framework based on shared structural principles across languages.
abstracts.010488: This paper addresses the issue of (semantic) pleonastic—or expletive—categories in natural lan- guages, with a focus on Italian, a language rich in such expressions. Pleonastic categories refer to elements that do not affect the truth-value conditions associated with a sentence. Examples include vocative particles, vocative phrases, coordination, expletive negations, and ethical datives. The paper presents a syntactic analysis showing that a “pleonastic/expletive” interpretation arises from a common structural configuration: these elements are directly merged in the complementizer domain (or higher), which prevents them from participating in the compositional semantics that determines propositional meaning. Instead, they contribute only to the interpretive layer, where discourse-level meanings are established. It follows that no truly semantically empty categories exist in the linguistic system; rather, their pleonastic or expletive semantics result from their syntactic configuration—and, in fact, they always retain some aspect of their original function.
abstracts.010489: Research on the Sino-Tibetan language family has spanned over a century . However, existing studies have largely remained within the linguistic domain, paying insufficient attention to the ecological transformations accompanying the diversification of Proto-Sino-Tibetan. This paper proposes an interdisciplinary methodology integrating archaeology, paleoclimatology, and natural history, organized around problem-driven inquiry rather than a single disciplinary paradigm,illustrated through specific lexical case studies. The Proto-Sino-Tibetan population can be broadly associated with the Peiligang-Yangshao cultural sequence, flourishing during the Holocene Climatic Optimum when Central China was approximately 2–3°C warmer than today, with tropical fauna such as Asian elephants, rhinoceroses, and Chinese alligators widely distributed. As Tibeto-Burman groups migrated onto the Tibetan Plateau, dramatic ecological shifts led to the loss of certain proto-roots, semantic drift, or substrate residue. Through case studies of elephant, rhinoceros, snake, crocodilian, millet, and agricultural tool terms, this paper demonstrates how ecological, climatic, and subsistence changes shaped Sino-Tibetan lexical evolution. Integrating molecular anthropological evidence, it further proposes that certain Tibetan terms for endemic species (e.g., yak g.yag, snow leopard gsa') may constitute substrate residue from D-lineage hunter-gatherer populations. This methodology, rooted in the natural history tradition while embracing modern scientific results, offers a new interdisciplinary perspective for Sino-Tibetan studies.Comments are welcome. 汉藏语系的相关研究，距今已经跨越百年。然而既有研究多囿于语言学范畴，对原始汉藏语分化过程中伴随的生态剧变关注不足。本文提出一种结合考古学、古气候学与博物学的跨学科研究方法，以“问题为中心”而非以单一学科范式为中心，并结合具体词例加以说明。 原始汉藏语人群大致归属裴李岗—仰韶文化序列，其生存时期正值全新世大暖期，中原地区 年均温较今高约 2—3℃，亚洲象、犀牛、扬子鳄等热带动物广泛分布。随着藏缅语人群迁 入青藏高原，生存生态发生显著变迁，导致部分祖语词根丢失、语义漂移或发生底层残留。 本文通过“大象”“犀牛”“蛇”“鳄”“粟黍”及农具类词例，论证生态—气候—生计方 式变迁对汉藏语词汇演变的影响；并结合分子人类学证据，提出藏语中部分本土物种词汇（如牦牛 g.yag、雪豹 gsa'）可能为 D 系狩猎采集人群的底层残留。该方法论根植于博物学传统，兼容现代技术成果，旨在为汉藏语系研究提供新的跨学科视角。欢迎批评指正。
abstracts.010490: This squib concerns fake indexicals, i.e., 1st and 2nd person pronouns interpreted as bound variables. Speciﬁcally, it examines two well-known contrasts between fake indexicals associated with focus in matrix clauses and in so-called Partee sentences— relative clauses introduced by who. I argue that the locus of the cross-linguistic variation lies in which phase head has the capacity to transmit features (building on insights from Kratzer 2009, Wurmbrand 2017b, among others). The distribution is further mediated by features of the relative pronoun in the language. Englishinternal variation is a function of derivational timing, with the contribution of focus (modeled via the Exh operator of Fox 2007) playing a critical role. I suggest that, despite the differences, the Exh mechanism and the feature-transmission mechanism may be formally related: merging the Exh operator at the phase edge yields a syntactic representation that is a special case of a more general feature-uniﬁcation procedure induced on the feature structure of a phase head.

abstracts.010493: This paper contributes to the debate on how grammatical marking shapes discourse management. Focusing on Differential Object Marking (DOM) in Levantine Arabic, we argue that DOM in this language signals the asserted proposition as a non-default Discourse Commitment (Gunlogson, 2001; Farkas and Bruce, 2010). We show that DOM triggers a range of interpretive outcomes–including emotive content, corrections, accommodations, and activating parallel Questions Under Discussion–and that the concept of a non-default Discourse Commitment accurately captures this diversity. Building on Zarka (2024), who proposes that the syntactic structure of DOM supports an aboutness topicality interpretation and provides an anaphoric anchor for adding the proposition to the Table (a discourse-tracking device), we explain why not all aboutness topics in the language yield these effects. We contend that the additional illocutionary force arises from economy considerations (Sichel and Wiltschko, 2021), because a simpler structure could otherwise express the same denotation. Our proposal reﬁnes our understanding of the structural underpinnings of non-default Discourse Commitments and underscores the role of anaphoricity in this process.
abstracts.010494: This paper investigates a correlation between copula agreement and anaphoric potential in Czech and German copular clauses. We argue that this correlation stems from a structural ambiguity between standard predicational clauses and a novel category of classificatory clauses. To capture the intuition that nominal predicates in the latter act as classifiers rather than simple property-denoting expressions, we introduce Locus Semantics. By distinguishing between an entity and its mental representation (locus), this framework allows for a formal treatment of grammatical features as class-presuppositions. We propose that while predicational structures resolve conflicting class-presuppositions via a type-shifter—allowing only for accommodated anaphora—classificatory structures utilize a silent, mediating pronoun. This pronoun introduces a distinct locus, thereby licensing non-canonical agreement and direct discourse anaphora.
abstracts.010495: Czech, the West Slavic language at the centre of our investigation, employs two varieties of stand-alone demonstratives. The first type is an agreeing demonstrative ten/ta/to…‘this.m.sg/f.sg/n.sg’ that agrees with 𝜙-features of its antecedent, whenever these are available. This standalone demonstrative is strictly referential, and in general displays common cross-linguistic behaviour. 1 Our focus will be on the other type: the non-agreeing variant, which we dub to, based on its Nominative form. This stand-alone demonstrative is always realized as neuter singular, irrespective of the gender and number of its antecedent. Previous literature has characterized to as the Czech equivalent of English it, either as a ‘nonperson’ pronoun (Hlavsa 1975, building on Mathesius 1926, 1943), or as a situation pronoun (Bartošová & Kučerová, 2014; Kučerová & Bartošová, 2016; Bartošová, 2017). The empirical support for this comparison comes from the observation that to is mostly restricted to inanimate antecedents. Yet, it allows animate antecedents in a limited set of environments. Moreover, to seems to combine properties of a referential pronoun and a situation-denoting pronoun. This paper argues that what distinguishes these two demonstrative types is not their internal makeup but their position in the structure. In particular, we will assume without further discussion that the agreeing type occupies an argument position, and in turn can be accounted for by, for example, Panagiotidis (2002), building on Postal (1969), and Elbourne (2008). We argue, however, that to is not an argument. Instead, to is an overt topical element merged in the MiddleField (Frey, 2000). We will use this structural configuration to explain the mixed referential behaviour attested with to. Under our account this mixed behaviour is not a property of to itself but arises from an interaction with a covert pronoun bound by to, the actual argument. The proposal explains some puzzling restrictions on the syntactic distribution and interpretation of to in quantificational environments, copular clauses, and wh-questions, and advances our understanding of topic environments and of the covert elements employed in them.
abstracts.010496: This paper describes a process of laryngeal reduction in San Martín Peras Mixtec (SMPM; ISO: jmx), an Otomanguean language spoken in Oaxaca and by diasporic communities throughout Mexico and the US. In this process, roots containing a laryngealized vowel often appear in a highly reduced form in fast speech. Laryngeal reduction is gradient, dependent on speech rate, and lacks a phonologically defined conditioning environment, giving it the characteristics of a phonetic process. However, it is at least sometimes correlated with a phonological process of mora deletion, as evidenced by the fact that some highly reduced laryngealized roots—but no unreduced laryngealized roots—undergo a phonological tone sandhi alternation that applies only to mono-moraic rising tones. The phonological process of mora deletion is argued to be conditioned by the same phonetic factors that drive laryngeal reduction, constituting an instance of a phonological process triggered by purportedly phonetic factors.
abstracts.010497: The posture of the larynx modulates fundamental frequency mechanically, and this linkage underlies a robust typological association between voicing, pitch, and phonation across the world’s languages. A long tradition of phonological theory explains the association by encoding laryngeal substance in tonal features. This article argues that the explanation fails. One laryngeal source is phonologized as categorically distinct objects, as tone, voice register, ballistic stress, or phrasal melody, varying language by language. Once phonologized, tonal categories can detach from their phonetic origins, patterning as abstract classes rather than according to their phonetic correlates. The association be- tween voice and tone is not a matter of representational content; it is explained by diachrony, in the mechanics of the larynx and the channel of transmission through which sound systems pass during acquisition. Phonological representations are most adequately viewed as abstract, substance-free, emergent, and language-specific, relieved of an explanatory burden they cannot meet.
abstracts.010498: Northern Iroquoian languages are famous for the complexities of their agreement systems, realized through three sets of ‘pronominal prefixes’. Drawing on new and existing material from Kanien’kéha (Mohawk), this article proposes a formal model that captures the range of empirical patterns using standard assumptions about argument structure and agreement, combined with the proposal that inanimate nominals have no person, number, or gender (φ) features and are thus invisible to the agreement system. This result is important in light of the fact that Kanien’kéha and its close relative Oneida have been the subject of proposals for major parametric variation among human languages. In The polysynthesis parameter, Baker (1996) draws primarily on Kanien’kéha, arguing that a macroparameter relating to the realization of agreement morphology is responsible for a range of morphosyntactic phenomena in Kanien’kéha and other polysynthetic languages. Koenig and Michelson (2015) examine agreement puzzles in Oneida and argue for a different type of macroparameter: that Northern Iroquoian languages differ from other languages in lacking a level of argument structure and local syntactic selection altogether. In this article, I argue that the core empirical patterns can be captured through the proposal that inanimate nominals are featureless, and that reference to hierarchical structure is necessary to capture the full range of facts. The absence of φ-features on inanimates in turn has implications both for the typology of nominal features and for the Polysynthesis Parameter, a parameter that requires all arguments in polysynthetic languages to be morphologically referenced on the verb.
abstracts.010499: This paper shows that within possible world semantics (PWS), any principled attempt to identify the common content of two beliefs based on notions such as subject-matter or maximal informativeness ultimately requires an appeal to the Axiom of Choice (AC). While PWS can plausibly assume that shared content exists, it cannot construct it. We contrast this with truthmaker semantics (TMS), where common content can instead be explicitly constructed from the truthmakers of the input propositions, via two independently motivated and equivalent constructions, without invoking AC. We take this to argue that axiomatic parsimony, e.g., whether a framework must assume the existence of certain entities rather than construct them, constitutes a novel dimension along which semantic theories can be compared, and suggest that this difference may be linked to whether a framework's basic entities carry mereological structure.
abstracts.010501: This study explores how various discourse structures influence the identity formation of non-native speakers as ESL learners and teachers within a specified time and space. Discourse is understood as an organizing and coherent system of knowledge expressed through linguistic means and praxis (Pavlenko, 2003). It embodies particular perspectives and encompasses the ways of associating in which tools, thoughts, words, values, and objects are associated and systematized in specific times and spaces for the purpose of constructing and recognizing and identities and practices. The study is based on a real-life account of a multilingual student proficient in several languages such as English, Sindhi, Urdu, Siraiki, Punjabi, and Hindi. The essay examines the role and significance of both dominant and alternative discourses in shaping the learner’s identity throughout her experiences of learning and teaching English in her native country. Four discourses are discussed: the discourse of native speakers and Standard English, the non-native speaker or L2 learner identity, the appropriation of a multilingual identity, and the discourse of classroom interaction. These discourses frame the ways individuals think about the experience particular practices and phenomena; they have historically dominated English educational contexts and have shaped—and reshaped—learner identity over time. The findings support Cook’s (1999) concept of multicompetence, which envisions an imagined community for multilinguals and positions second language learners as empowered and legitimate users of the target language. In light of these findings, translanguaging pedagogy is recommended as an effective approach for adapting instructional practices within multilingual contexts
