abstracts.010504: Speakers of the same language draw category boundaries in slightly different places. A color chip that most speakers call green may therefore be called blue by others. Disagreement of this kind is usually treated as noise: typological mode maps retain only each chip's majority term, and labeling pipelines combine annotations by majority vote. Disagreement also carries a cost for communication, but for a learner who has access only to names, the direction of disagreement records which categories are neighbors. Departures from the majority happen mostly near boundaries and almost always use the term for the category on the other side. A simple model compares this evidence with the cost to a listener: as the spread of boundaries decreases, the listener's extra error decreases quadratically, while the learner's evidence about neighboring categories decreases only linearly. We test this account with small language models trained only on object-naming sentences. In an artificial language with a known scale, their object representations reflect the scale only when speakers' boundaries differ. In 92 languages of the World Color Survey, randomly replacing the minority terms while preserving where and how often departures occur reduces the recoverable color geometry in every language for the naming text and in 90–92 languages for the models. Retaining only the majority term removes this geometry.
abstracts.010505: In this paper, I describe syntax and semantics of Marathi polar questions and polar questions particles to place them on the broader Indo-Aryan landscape. In doing so, I argue that Marathi polar question particles uniformly signal information-seeking polar questions when clause-final, while their clause-medial occurrences – wherever grammatical – signal non-canonical questions of various kinds. I show that this indicates a strict mapping between the syntactic and semantic-pragmatic notions of canonicity of questions and necessitates a closer examination of semantic-pragmatic properties of clause-medial polar question particles from Indo-Aryan languages previously described in the literature.
abstracts.010506: This paper explores the possible derivational pathways to the phenomenon known as pied-piping with inversion (PPwI), through the lens of possessor extraction in Sm’algyax (Tsimshianic; British Columbia/Alaska). I first consider two derivational pathways that differ in how the wh-word comes to precede the possessed noun, and more generally, how the wh-possessive constituent comes to occupy clause-initial position. In the standard “inversion” analysis (e.g., Aissen 1996; Coon 2009), these properties are derived through two steps of Ā-movement. In the “no inversion” analysis (Royer et al. 2026), they arise from the base-generation of a wh-word in the form of a non-verbal predicate together with operator movement inside the wh-predicate’s clausal complement. I argue that although Sm’algyax independently permits both wh-movement and wh-predication, possessor extraction nevertheless requires an inversion step. I then show that such configurations are compatible with a base-generated wh-predicate analysis.
abstracts.010507: Although prepositional infinitives (PIs) are generally rare in Spanish as these are selected mainly by reflexive verbs and non-reflexive verbs tend to select the bare infinitive in accordance with verbal argument structure (Green (1988:109-110), Subirats-Rüggeberg (1987:4ff)), PIs headed by de are attested as complements of non-reflexive verbs in Spanish dialects in parallel to other Romance varieties. This phenomenon known as el deísmo displays microvariation between peninsular and Latin American varieties (Castillo-Ros (2017a)): in the former (Andalucía, La Mancha) de-infinitives are selected in a range of constructions that have parallels in other Romance languages and older stages of Spanish (Di Tullio (2011, 2013), Camus Bergareche (2013), Benito and Pato (2015)), whereas in the latter (grammatical for speakers from Perú and Ecuador, acceptable for speakers from Chile and Venezuela) de-infinitives are used only in the passive of Exceptional Case-Marking (ECM) constructions and not in the active (Montalbetti (1999)), which suggests that el deísmo can be parameterised between peninsular and Latin American Spanish in terms of grammatical voice (active and passive respectively). While the historical-comparative distribution of de-infinitives suggests that these PIs stem from proto-Romance/Latin, especially Latin prepositional gerund(ive)s which suppletively represent the oblique relations of the infinitive and are collocated with the relevant lexical verbs (Vincent (1988:68-70, 1999:4-6), Schulte (2007:79, 87-90, 106-109)), the retention of de in the passivisation of Latin American ECM-constructions is striking evidence that de is essential for ECM A(rgument)-raising (cf Castillo Ros (2017b)), which is traditionally formalised as the raising of the subject of the embedded infinitive to the matrix subject position via a matrix object-position (Lasnik (1999, 2001)). In a Phase-theoretic approach (Chomsky (2000, 2001)) where Phase-Impenetrability Condition (PIC) makes it necessary for the raised argument to be visible to the matrix verb (Sheehan and Cyrino (2018)), this is possible only if the infinitival complement projects an extra projection (i.e. not bare infinitive) as is attested cross-linguistically (Borgonovo (1996), Felser (1998, 1999), Hornstein, Nunes and Martins (2008)), which can be determined to be de (Fin(ite)/M(ood)) (cf Rizzi (1997)). In this framework, it is possible to parameterise el deísmo in terms of two structural positions: SpecFin/M and SpecAppl(icative), both of which are essential for the passivisation and A-raising in ECM-constructions. While de (M) provides an escape-hatch (SpecFin/M) for the embedded subject to move to the matrix clause, it can be argued that peninsular Spanish varieties do not project ApplP while Latin American ones do, which can explain why passivisation of ECM verbs is possible in the latter and not in the former. Moreover, in this derivational model where the infinitive needs to be ‘big’ in order to facilitate A-raising of the embedded subject, the Spanish infinitive seems to be relatively ‘small’ in contrast to other Romance languages (e.g. Italian where the bare infinitive permits ECM A-raising) as an overt complementizer (de) is required to allow A-raising of the embedded subject to the matrix clause (Sheehan (2023)).
abstracts.010508: Focus semantics is intimately linked with question semantics, but syntactically the two phenomena come apart in English and other European languages: while at least one wh-phrase in questions must move to an ex-situ, sentence-initial position, foci generally remain in situ. This has led to two different accounts being widely adopted for focus and question semantics: on the one hand, an in-situ semantics for focus that assigns a set meaning for the focussed constituent and point-wise composition projects the set meaning to higher phrasal constituents; on the other hand, an ex-situ semantics for questions that assumes movement of wh-phrases above a question complementizer that takes a propositional argument to describe a set of propositions. Though it is well known that an in-situ semantics like that for focus can also be provided for questions—in fact, the alternative semantics for questions is even older than the alternative semantics for focus (Hamblin, 1973)—the opposite is not widely known: an ex-situ semantics for focus like the standard semantics for questions. This type of semantics is presented below.
abstracts.010509: Existing approaches to deontic modality, directives, and social relations provide important resources for analyzing prohibition, but a compositional question remains: how does a lexical prohibition report relate an actual normative eventuality to an intensional target and to the authority of its source? Focusing on Mandarin jìnzhǐ `prohibit', we develop an event-based deontic semantics that distinguishes the norm-bearing eventuality from the possible target event and uses source--addressee jurisdiction to constrain the selection of negative requirements. The resulting analysis derives an event-relative deontic obligation without entailing either compliance or violation in the actual world. It also distinguishes normative addressees from embedded thematic agents, accommodating both interpersonal prohibitions and institutional restrictions on non-agentive eventualities. We thus show how event relativity and socially grounded authority jointly contribute to the lexical semantics of prohibition.
abstracts.010510: Camuno is a dialect of Eastern Lombard characterized by stress-driven high vowel harmony where all mid vowels preceding stressed [i] and round ones preceding stressed [u] rise. The low central [a] does not participate in the harmony and is opaque, that is, preceding vowels also do not participate in the harmony. However, a pattern of transparency of [a] is attested in the language. In this pilot study, I investigate the possible correlation between perceived fluency and acceptability of transparent [a] in Camuno. The results reveal a clear tendency to (perceptual) hyper-dialectalism by younger and less fluent speakers, which I argue to be motivated by the specificities of the sociolinguistic context where Camuno is spoken. In addition to describing an emerging pattern of micro-variation, the results open questions about the role of hyper-dialectalism as a driving force for language change in the context of dilalia (Berruto, 1987). [This is an initial pilot study, comments and suggestions are very welcome]
abstracts.010511: Bacon et al. 2023 argue that Upper Palaeolithic mark sequences track the seasonal timing of animal reproductive cycles and so represent the earliest evidence for the use of an abstract notation system representing information, at least twenty-six thousand years ago, over twenty thousand years before the earliest Sumerian writing system. This paper evaluates the validity of those claims by subjecting the original dataset to rigorous statistical re-analyses. It addresses the methodological critiques raised in subsequent literature by i) clarifying the original species-level statistical analysis, ii) reporting previously omitted right-to-left sign positional data, iii) discussing the most appropriate unit of analysis to be employed in statistical tests of this data, iv) explaining that the baseline probabilities of finding matches to birth or mating are known and differ between species, and v) presenting new sets of analyses using Poisson-Binomial tests and Monte-Carlo permutation tests both of which can take account of these issues. In addition, we rectify figure-generation alignment errors erroneously introduced in our original paper. Strong statistical associations persist between non- sequence lengths and mating periods, and between sign variables and birth windows. The principal quantitative findings of Bacon et al. thus remain robust.
abstracts.010512: This descriptive chapter provides an overview of the major patterns of subordinate clause formation in Tigrinya, with particular attention to the morphosyntactic markers that introduce relative, adverbial, and complement clauses. Tigrinya employs a small set of clausal prefixes, z(ɨ)-, k(ɨ)-, and kämz(ɨ)-, whose distribution cuts across traditional clause-type distinctions and correlates with syntactic and semantic differences. Relative clauses are formed with z(ɨ)-, which also appears in a range of adverbial and embedded constructions. Complement clauses may be introduced by kämz(ɨ)- or k(ɨ)- triggering in some cases distinct interpretive properties. The chapter situates these patterns within broader discussions of subordination in Ethio-Semitic and Semitic syntax.
abstracts.010513: We investigate the behavior of the Italian verbs ‘must’, ‘can’, and ‘want’, which come in two syntactic guises. Against the view that modals like ‘must’ and ‘can’ are raising verbs, we use evidence from an impersonal construction with the clitic si to argue for an analysis in terms of control and functional restructuring. The proposal allows for a unified syntactic treatment of the three verbs and provides a transparent dissociation of syntactic and semantic properties.
abstracts.010514: Belk et al. (2023) and Barros and Vicente (2011) have argued that Right-Node Raising (RNR) requires a dual analysis, as either multidominance or ellipsis. This paper examines RNR at the subword level (e.g., over- and undergenerate) and shows that, like phrasal RNR, subword RNR displays mixed properties diagnostic of both multidominance and ellipsis, supporting a dual analysis at both levels. We argue, however, that the dual approach, as currently implemented, cannot capture certain subword and phrasal RNR data without modification. We therefore propose a modified version of RNR-as-ellipsis, in which focus-marked material can survive ellipsis in situ, and which captures both subword and phrasal RNR, while retaining multidominance as the second component of the dual analysis.
abstracts.010515: This paper addresses the syntactic differences between Italian participial passives (p-pass) and si-passives (s-pass). Both involve a syntactically projected implicit external argument, which licenses depictives and non-logophoric anaphors, but only in p-pass can this argument receive a definite interpretation or alternate with a by-phrase. Furthermore, only the s-pass implicit argument creates intervention effects in the dependency between T and the internal argument. I propose that these differences stem from the fact that the promotion of the internal argument relies on Collins’ (2005) smuggling only in p-pass, and not in s-pass: this can also explain the different availability of inalienable possession readings in the two constructions.
abstracts.010516: This chapter reviews the relevant literature on scrambling, focusing on three central issues raised by this phenomenon: (i) the relationship between scrambling and free word order—or, framed differently, the base-generation versus movement approaches to scrambling (section 2); (ii) the configurational/positional properties of three distinct scrambling types, namely, VP-internal, clause-internal, and long-distance scrambling (section 3); and (iii) potential triggers for scrambling as a movement operation (section 4). In addition, this chapter addresses ongoing developments in research on scrambling, focusing on how the very option of scrambling is permitted from the perspective of labeling (i.e., Saito 2016, 2018) (section 5). The chapter also explores whether scrambling necessitates movement/Internal Merge, or whether its putative effects can instead be captured through non-movement algorithms such as Minimal Search, following latest extensions of the MP (i.e., Kitahara 2026) (section 6).
abstracts.010517: Self-destructive feeding (SDF) is a type of overapplication opacity in which, in rule-based terms, an earlier rule creates the environment for a later rule that in turn removes part of the environment that motivated the earlier one. This paper re-examines four cases of SDF (two in Turkish, one in Javanese and one in Japanese) and shows that they can be accounted for in Parallel Optimality Theory. After introducing the four cases, the paper presents the two properties they share. First, at least one of the processes involved in each interaction is restricted to morpheme junctures and particular morphemes. Second, they resolve consonant sequences at stem-suffix junctures by realising a suffix-initial segment in required contexts. I propose that the alternating segments are underspecified for their association to the skeletal tier, whereas non-alternating segments are fully-specified. In Parallel Optimality Theory, faithfulness to association in general and stronger faithfulness in certain input contexts or positions then account for the lack of morpheme-internal alternations and the SDF outputs in a single input--output evaluation. The three SDF cases involving consonants follow from the rankings needed for the simple alternations alone, and the vowel case requires only one additional ranking. Therefore, SDF involving alternations with zero can be derived in Parallel Optimality Theory once the underlying representations of segments are more appropriately understood.
abstracts.010518: Poetic metres govern the basic rhythmic patterns of verses and lines, and generally require the phonological property they regulate (e.g. stress, weight and/or tone) to alternate within a line to avoid monotony. Using the tonal metre of Middle Chinese regulated verse as an example, this paper proposes that a metre can also require the regulated property not to alternate, and that this requirement is balanced against alternation. The canonical templates of regulated verse require tone categories to alternate within a line, but only to a restricted extent: no non-final syllable in the templates is flanked by two syllables of the opposite category. Beyond the templates, the paper shows in Optimality Theory that the remedies prescribed by traditional prosody for irregular lines follow from the interaction of constraints encoding alternation and non-alternation. The two remedies for guping ‘Lone Even’ (孤平) are outputs of different rankings within a single, partially ranked grammar: the remedy within the line satisfies a non-alternation constraint against a lone Even tone, whereas the remedy in the other line of the couplet satisfies an alternation constraint requiring the two lines of a couplet to be tonal opposites (对). The ‘three-inversion-four-remedy’ pattern (三拗四救) arises when alternation in the cadence of a line takes priority over faithfulness. Finally, I show that this balancing property enriches the typology of poetic metres and parallels restrictions found in the tonal phonology of natural languages, and that metres can be informed by – and thus serve as a window into – natural language phonology.
abstracts.010519: This squib reports a previously undescribed restriction on the Albanian distributive marker nga. While nga combines freely with numeral expressions, speakers judge it strongly degraded with the quantifier shumë ‘many’. An acceptability judgment experiment confirms a selective interaction between distributive marking and quantifier type: the presence of nga lowers acceptability with shumë ‘many’, but not with numerals. Additional judgments suggest that related restrictions may extend to other quantity expressions and to distributive markers in other languages. At the same time, some imprecise numeral expressions appear more acceptable. These findings suggest that distributive marking is not uniformly compatible with all quantity expressions, raising broader questions about how such constructions interact with vagueness.
abstracts.010520: This volume brings together recent work by a new generation of scholars on the formal semantic and pragmatic analysis of Chinese languages. Rather than presenting a comprehensive handbook, the volume offers a curated snapshot of an expanding field, showing how Chinese data can illuminate central questions in semantic theory. The chapters cover a wide range of topics, including quantification, classifiers, telicity, incompleteness, temporal reference, modality, causation, degree semantics, scalar particles, wh-constructions, biased questions, clefts, and sentence-final particles. Across these domains, the volume demonstrates how formal tools can sharpen long-standing insights into Chinese grammar while opening new directions for cross-linguistic comparison. Combining theoretical modeling with diverse empirical evidence – including introspective judgments, corpus data, experimental findings, processing evidence, typological comparisons, and dialectal fieldwork – this book highlights the richness of Chinese as a testing ground for formal semantics. It will be of interest to researchers and graduate students in formal semantics, pragmatics, Chinese linguistics, and cross-linguistic semantic theory. [The volume will be officially pulished on November 24, 2026: https://www.routledge.com/New-Perspectives-on-Chinese-Formal-Semantics/Luo-Li/p/book/9781041207672]
abstracts.010521: The overview literature distinguishes two OTs, which I call bare bone OT (BB-OT) and lingua franca OT (LF-OT). The former reduces to the initial idea: GEN + EVAL, i.e. parallel computation carried out by constraint interaction. The latter is a theory of everything (expansionist, says Iosad 2018): a franchise where anybody can plug in add-ons of any kind that serve a specific purpose, van Oostendorp (2021) says, pursuing that "[f]or many phonologists, OT offers a notation system for writing theories rather than anything else" (p.553). This also reflects the fact that OT is not a theory of phonology, but rather a theory of computation, or decision making, that may as well be applied to physics, chemistry, sociology, management, well-being, etc. BB-OT appears when the superfluous layers peel back. This evolution occurred since 1993: the doctrinal body that OT went on stage with dissolved – none of the initial promises are made good on. Most prominently, the claim that computation is exclusively parallel is abandoned: it is trivial and fully uncontroversial today that there are serial elements among different constraint rankings (Stratal OT) and/or within a given ranking (OT-CC). The same goes for all other design properties like Freedom of Analysis, Richness of the Base, violability of constraints, free ranking, the innateness and universality of the constraint set, dominance, surface-orientation or the belonging of constraints to either the markedness or the faithfulness family: all this is gone. Gone in the sense that ignoring or violating these principles is commonplace and trivial. Doing that or not is a matter of taste which leaves the OT community entirely unimpressed – nobody reacts: the items at hand have become irrelevant. Based on a tabula rasa narrative, OT thus started with assumptions breaking with insights that phonology had accumulated since the Neogrammarians, but 33 years later is back to square one, i.e. to some version of the pre-OT take (like serialism). The other major evolution of OT concerns the empiricist heritage of connectionism (which is not discussed in the overview literature). While Prince & Smolensky (1993, section 10.2) reject all connectionist tenets save one (parallel computation), over the years about all others found their way into the theory, undermining OT's rationalist generative intention. Some items of the connectionist toolbox such as gradience entered overtly: connection weight in the guise of weighted constraints, activation threshold later on under the heading of gradient symbolic representations. But gradience also moved in more generally, as acoustic formant values, probabilistic candidate evaluation or Max-Ent. The structuralist and generative point of view is that gradience does not live in grammar, though (it bears on speech by shaping its output, Du & Durvasula 2024). In generative quarters outside of OT, there is no gradience in grammar: for instance, no syntactician would consider something like "0.7 plural" (as opposed to "1.2 plural"). Other connectionist essentials sneaked on board as silent passengers. This is the case of anti-symbolism (which was explicitly rejected by Prince & Smolensky 1993): connectionist computation is colorless, i.e. uses the same input (levels of energy) for the computation of anything (vision, phonology, attention, emotions, etc.). The rationalist take, modularity, is symbolic and characterizes the generative view since day one: different computational systems process distinct, domain-specific vocabulary. OT systematically violates modularity by hosting morphological, phonological and phonetic factors in the same constraint ranking (or even the same constraint: ALIGN). Together with the fact that OT is a theory of computation that has nothing to say about representations, anti-symbolism was also at work when representations became zombies: still around, but dead. That is, the objects computed are irrelevant and interchangeable, only computation (constraint interaction) decides about grammaticality. In sum, LF-OT is incompatible with the generative view on many counts. This is the case of two design properties present in 1993: the incapacity to express universals and the fact just mentioned that grammaticality is decided exclusively by computation (in the constraint chamber). Two other serious offenders of generative settings emerged as OT developed: the import of gradience and functional factors into grammar. These directions could be taken because there are no constraints on constraints. This is a gateway for anything to be located in grammar: behavioural categories (LAZY), psycho-linguistic or social factors (*UMC[t]/*LMC[t]: [t] is socially marked in the speech of upper/lower middle-class speakers) and so on. OT is not liable for individual practitioners setting up constraints about the upper middle class etc., but it is responsible for allowing these choices to be possible in the first place. In comparison, rule-based computation disqualifies them: rules are unable to accommodate anything but truly phonological vocabulary: there is no way to write a rule that contains phonology-alien elements, such as p,t,k → lazy / __V, or V → ə / upper middle class. This contrast between OT and the rest of the generative enterprise also strikes the eye when considering the opposite directions that OT and generative syntax have taken in their contemporary evolution in the 90s: while the heart of minimalism is to free grammar from anything that can be explained by extra-linguistic factors (leaving behind only core syntax), OT loaded grammar with extra-phonological and extra-linguistic factors. OT's internal evolution has eliminated the two obstacles for meeting generative standards that were present in 1993, and the idea that gradience and functional factors are located in grammar are choices that one does not need to make. A generative implementation of OT is possible in the guise of BB OT, though: parallel computation managed by GEN and EVAL (supplemented with a serial element) may be put to use in a setting where gradience and functional factors are banned from grammar, reference is only made to phonological objects (i.e. modularity is respected) and representations are equal-righted, rather than zombies: they are not reducible to computation and contribute their own arbitral award. This approach is then a competitor for traditional rule-based computation where computation is i) only serial (i.e. has no parallel component), ii) based on rewrite rules (which is not the case of the serial element in OT-CC for example) and iii) supplemented with hard (i.e. non-violable) constraints on the output (well-formedness conditions). These issues will then make the competition and need to be debated. Severing the connectionist ties of OT may thus reinstantiate a generative theory of computation, BB-OT, which leaves LF-OT wandering into the unchartered space of a theory of everything (and thus of nothing, i.e. a mere notational system).
abstracts.010522: Nested which -questions such as "Which album by which band do you like best?" lack the so-called 'pair-list' reading which is otherwise available for ordinary multiple questions (Higginbotham & May 1981; Elliott 2015b; Fox & Sudo 2025). We show that the scopal theory of pied-piping (Charlow 2019; Demirok 2019) nevertheless derives such readings, even if the contained which -phrase is barred from subextracting: the contained which -phrase can pied-pipe its container, which then reconstructs and takes scope over a second question nucleus, yielding a family of questions. In order to address this, we propose that covert QP-movement is subject to Chomsky's (1964) A-over-A condition, which blocks exactly these derivations while preserving the theory's account of pied-piping. Our proposal makes novel predictions beyond strict nesting, e.g., in what we call quasi-nesting configurations and for Baker's ambiguity. We argue these predictions are borne out, and that they distinguish our account from Fox & Sudo's (2025). The result is a case study in how highly expressive, semantically motivated compositional machinery can be constrained by independently motivated syntactic principles.
abstracts.010523: he paper provides an account of the case system as it is found in Khoekhoe, a Khoe language. In this language, in the clausal domain, nominals can only get Nominative case when contained in the canonical subject position at the left periphery of the clause. When appearing outside this position, subjects are marked in Object case, similarly to objects and other non-subject arguments. Furthermore, in interrogative clauses, Nominative case is unavailable on all DPs, including subjects, with nominals getting Object marking. I suggest that Nominative in Khoekhoe is assigned by the C head in the SpecCP position with the C in being able to trigger both A and ¯A movement causing bottleneck effects, which prevents subjects from getting Nominative case when the SpecCP position is occupied by another phrase. For interrogative clauses, I assume that the SpecCP in such cases must be obligatorily occupied by an ¯A moved constituent, which effectively bleeds Nominative marking in suchcontexts. I suggest that ¯A moved phrases may be of DP, PP, AdvP and also of verbal (vP) size. In this way, Khoekhoe can be seen as an example of a language where V2 effects have consequences for caseassignment.
abstracts.010524: The goal of this squib is to draw attention to a side effect that recent work in mathematical linguistics has for phonology. Graf (2022) demotes the computational complexity of syntax from (at least) Regular to Subregular because of the understanding that syntax does not generate linear strings (as was taken for granted before), but rather trees. This is in line with the leading Minimalist idea that linearity, being imposed by the interfaces, is absent from syntax. As a result, the empirical difference between syntactic and phonological patterns does not stem from computational complexity anymore (since phonology is also Subregular), but rather from the fact that syntax builds trees, while phonology outputs linear strings. That is, there are no trees in phonology. On the phonological side, alternatives to arboreal structure in phonology have emerged since the 2000s. The squib spotlights this convergence: recent developments in mathematical linguistics support the lateral perspective on phonology, meaning that there is no tree-building device in this module. Thus, hierarchy in language is implemented in module-specific ways: trees in syntax, lateral relations in phonology. This distribution is argued to stem from the design properties of the two modules: syntax is based on Merge and Merge creates trees, while phonology is linear in kind. Lateral relations could not exist in syntax because there is no linearity; trees do not exist in phonology because there is no Merge.
abstracts.010525: In the 20th and early 21st centuries, linguists developed techniques for studying syntactic competence and syntactic processing in humans. A key underlying assumption of this work was that all humans who have acquired a language in the typical way are syntactically competent. For much of this period, it was also obvious that machine systems were not syntactically competent. With the rise of Language Models that could seemingly produce and comprehend utterances in human language, this latter assumption was challenged. As a result, there was an explosion of work using the experimental syntax toolkit not to study syntactic processing in competent humans, but rather to ask whether Language Models had emergently developed syntactic competence. This research program proved fruitful, with the study of Language Model syntax now even offering testable hypotheses about human syntax. Here, we tell that story and argue that, while experimental work uncovered major lacunas in syntactic processing in earlier Language Models, modern Language Models have meaningfully acquired syntax.
abstracts.010526: Based on Chesterman’s (2009) work on translator studies, this article aims to outline a methodological approach to studying a translator and the influence of their life on the text. It does so on the example of a Polish translator, Róża Centnerszwerowa (1867–1940), who is “brought out” from what Venuti (2008) referred to as the shadow of the source-text author. In this study, events from the translator’s life are juxtaposed with excerpts from her translations and her translation output to emphasize that just as an author’s life is reflected in their texts, a translator’s experiences also influence their translations. The analysis is conducted on both a macro level — covering her entire body of work — and a micro level — focusing on the content of individual translations. This study complements the current knowledge about Centnerszwerowa and highlights the importance of research in translator studies by providing further methodological suggestions.
abstracts.010527: Brazilian Portuguese (BP) is traditionally analyzed as a language that categorically disallows preposition stranding, contrasting sharply with Germanic systems like English. However, natural corpus and vernacular data reveal that a small, highly specified set of prepositions—specifically sem 'without', contra 'against', and sobre 'on/about'—frequently surface without any phonologically overt DP complement in various syntactic domains. These configurations, termed "orphan prepositions," challenge long-standing typological generalizations regarding the nominal and prepositional architecture of Romance. This paper develops a comprehensive minimalist account demonstrating that BP does not instantiate English-type preposition stranding via extraction. Instead, orphaning constructions emerge from the structural interplay of null pronominal objects (pro), a distinct lexical-functional asymmetry within the prepositional system, and head movement parameterized as D-to-P incorporation. Expanding upon the [P+D] fusion framework, this paper tracks how phi-feature valuation and PF-erasure interact under phase-theoretic locality and anti-locality constraints. Ultimately, the syntax of BP orphan prepositions is shown to unify naturally with orphaning in French and inflected preposition paradigms in Semitic and Celtic languages, maintaining universal restrictions like the Head Movement Constraint.
abstracts.010528: It is well known that standard de re belief reports can truthfully describe non-specific beliefs that are straightforwardly captured by de dicto reports. This paper examines doubly intensional attitude reports where the higher operator is believe and the lower is a non-attitudinal modal with a circumstantial modal base (e.g. should). The beliefs reported by such constructions are modal in nature. It is shown that, in such configurations, the expressive potential of de re reports is more limited than in standard cases: de re reports cannot truthfully describe purely non-specific modal beliefs that are straightforwardly captured by purely de dicto reports. Against these new facts, the paper examines the predictions of two main theories of de re reporting: the theory of res movement and the theory of concept generators. It is shown that only the theory of res movement makes the correct prediction while the theory of concept generators overgenerates. A new in situ analysis of de re reporting is proposed that captures the facts and avoids the unorthodox res-movement mechanism. The final part of the paper is a case study of Kaplan’s (1968) famous shortest spy problem (the inability of de re reports to truthfully describe beliefs in trivialities). This problem is modelled as a special case of the established inability of de re reports to truthfully describe purely non-specific modal beliefs. The shortest spy problem is thus presented as an example of a more general semantic phenomenon whose analysis need not rely on the obscure notion of acquaintance relations.
abstracts.010529: This paper argues on empirical as well as conceptual grounds against a popular pragmatic account of cessation inferences triggered by past statives. It proposes an alternative account according to which cessation inferences are entailments rather than implicatures.
abstracts.010530: Contrastive genre analysis facilitates cross-linguistic comparisons of genre structures, offering insights into underlying cultural and social conventions. Online music reviews remain notably underexplored in this realm. This study aims to address this gap by conducting a contrastive genre analysis of English and German online album reviews. The study makes use of a self-compiled Corpus of Album Reviews (CAR) amounting to 120 texts written between 2021 and 2023. It is subdivided into a sub‑corpus of English Album Reviews (EAR) and its German counterpart, a sub‑corpus of German Album Reviews (GAR), each of which encompasses 60 texts. Seven rhetorical moves were identified in the reviews. The rhetorical moves in English and German online album reviews were compared across three measures: their frequency, inclusion rates, and word coverage. The findings reveal that German critics highlight interpretive depth and review synthesis, whereas English writers focus on capturing the reader’s attention.
abstracts.010531: Some languages have future markers that are banned from or dispreferred in negative contexts. This results in situations of asymmetry in which certain grammatical distinctions made in the affirmative are unavailable in the negative. We propose a diachronic explanation for such asymmetries: future markers first grammaticalize in affirmative contexts and only later, if at all, spread to negative contexts, sometimes with a time lag of hundreds of years. During the period where a novel future marker occurs in the affirmative but is incompatible with negation, the synchronic situation is perforce one of asymmetry. We further argue that newly grammaticalized future markers tend to be banned from negative contexts due to their semantics and discourse function. New futures are typically immediate futures. We suggest that speakers conventionally use novel immediate futures to make their statements more informative. As a consequence, these future markers require the assertion to be stronger than its alternatives. In affirmative contexts, the use of an immediate future gives rise to a strong assertion. On the other hand, in negative contexts, the use of an immediate future leads to a weak assertion, which conflicts with the conventional discourse function of these markers. As a result, novel immediate futures tend to be restricted to affirmative contexts, i.e., they are positive polarity items.
abstracts.010532: The fact that impersonal transitive verbs can be passivised serves as a litmus test for any theory of passivisation. Both the approaches of Generative Grammar and those of functionalist schools fall short. Theories must prove their worth in difficult terrain. That is where their true value can best be assessed.
abstracts.010533: 本文是对 LingBuzz 所上传论文《一种跨学科方法于汉藏语系研究的运用》（lingbuzz/010489） 的补充。笔者将该文所运用的方法正式命名为“博物演算语言学”（Natural History Calculus Linguistics, NHCL）。 此处“演算”并非微积分，也不是依赖数学或计算机科学的数值计算，而是指一种多变量的、以逻辑和多学科方法论进行推断的研究路径。本文补充了两个案例：其一，“枭/猫头鹰”词可与嘉绒语组形式及古汉语 *ˁkiw 相互参证，并与泉护村遗址雕鸮跗跖骨的动物考古证据形成呼应；其二，藏药“皱叶绢毛苣”，藏文 srol gong 的高海拔分布与语义结构，使其更适宜被解释为可能的底层残留词，与牦牛、雪豹等案例。 同理。本文还结合《彝医药常用名词术语》中关于博物学与数理科学两大研究范式及其分化的论述，反思现代学术高度分科化、精深化所带来的视野窄化与概念异化问题。笔者并非主张复古，而是在承认分科深度之基础上，主张保留研究视野的广度与襟怀。 This note is a supplement and response to my LingBuzz paper, 《一种跨学科方法于汉藏语系研究的运用》 (“An Interdisciplinary Method for Sino-Tibetan Studies”) (lingbuzz/010489). It formalizes the method used there as Natural History Calculus Linguistics (NHCL). Here “calculus” does not mean differential or integral calculus, nor does it refer to computation dependent on mathematics or computer science; it denotes a multi-variable inferential procedure grounded in logic and multidisciplinary methodologies. The note adds two cases. First, the “owl” word (枭) can be cross-checked against Rgyalrongic forms and Old Chinese *ˁkiw, and further resonates with the zooarchaeological evidence of an eagle-owl tarsometatarsus from the Quanhucun site. Second, the Tibetan medicinal plant name srol gong (སོལ་ོལ་, 皱叶绢毛苣, Soroseris Stebbins) is better interpreted as a possible substrate residue, given its high-altitude distribution and semantic structure, in line with cases such as the yak and snow leopard. The note also draws on 《彝医药常用名词术语》 to reflect on the split between natural-history and mathematical-experimental paradigms, and on the narrowing of vision and conceptual alienation produced by modern over-specialization. The aim is not antiquarianism, but the retention of breadth and intellectual openness on the basis of disciplinary depth.
abstracts.010534: As in Collins (2024), going back at least to Chomsky (1957), short passives must contain a syntactically merged (then deleted/silent) agent. In effect, the language faculty, in the spirit of Collins and Kayne (2023), does not allow for what might have been called ‘late insertion in the semantics’.
abstracts.010535: Russian simplex disjunction ili is characterized as a positive polarity item (Szabolcsi 2004): the generalization is that it is unable to take narrow scope with respect to a clausemate negation. This first half of the paper presents a novel generalization that the PPI behavior of Russian simplex disjunction is only observed when its alternative with simplex homogeneous conjunction is felicitous and truth-conditionally equivalent to its missing reading. The finding supports an alternative-sensitive account of positive polarity anti-licensing. The second half of the paper argues that Russian conjunction i exhibits homogeneity effects due to lacking a disjunctive alternative, which is supported by its infelicity as an answer to a disjunctive polar question. Anti-licensing of Russian simplex disjunction arises as a subcase of oddness induced by presence of equivalent alternatives (Magri 2009, Spector 2014, Bar-Lev&Fox 2023): negated disjunctive sentences with a narrow scope interpretation are ruled out because the conjunctive alternative gets the reading they would. The negated conjunctive sentence, however, is not ruled out because the negated disjunctive sentence is not its alternative.
